articles.summary: 1XBET te ofrece el pronóstico del partido que enfrenta a Inglaterra y España en Wembley correspondiente a la jornada 1 del Grupo 3 de la Nations League
articles.body: Inglaterra arranca la Nations League dando continuidad al proyecto de Thomas Tuchel después de alcanzar las semifinales del Mundial 2026. La selección inglesa afronta esta edición con el objetivo de seguir creciendo bajo las órdenes del técnico alemán y tendrá un estreno de máxima exigencia en Wembley. Enfrente, estará una España que llega después de conquistar su segunda estrella mundial y, lógicamente, da continuidad a este ciclo. Favorito para el partido entre Inglaterra y España España afronta este encuentro con el impulso del título mundial y con Luis de la Fuente recién renovado como seleccionador hasta 2032. Además, cuenta con buenos antecedentes ante Inglaterra: ganó en su última visita a Wembley y también se impuso en la final de la Eurocopa 2024. El duelo se presenta, en cualquier caso, muy equilibrado para las casas de apuestas: 1XBET ofrece una cuota de 2.90 por la victoria de Inglaterra, 3.30 por el empate y 2.40 por el triunfo de España. Ambos equipos marcan El mercado de ambos equipos marcan aparece como una opción interesante en las apuestas deportivas. Especialmente, teniendo en cuenta la dinámica reciente de Inglaterra. El conjunto inglés ha cumplido este pronóstico en sus cinco últimos encuentros, mientras que España solamente lo ha hecho en uno de sus cinco partidos más recientes. Los antecedentes apuntan, por tanto, en direcciones diferentes... aunque el potencial ofensivo de ambas selecciones puede favorecer un encuentro con ocasiones en las dos áreas. 1XBET ofrece una cuota de 1.66 por el 'sí' y de 2.10 por el 'no'. Número total de goles (Over/Under) La línea de goles también muestra diferencias significativas entre los dos combinados. En los cinco últimos partidos de Inglaterra se han marcado más de 2.5 goles totales, mientras que este registro solamente se ha producido en dos de los cinco encuentros más recientes de España. La dinámica inglesa apunta hacia partidos con marcadores más elevados, aunque el conjunto de Luis de la Fuente presenta una tendencia más contenida. 1XBET paga a 1.88 que se superen los 2.5 goles y a 1.92 que se registren menos de 2.5 tantos. Goles en ambas mitades El mercado de goles en ambas mitades presenta una tendencia idéntica en los dos equipos. En tres de los cinco últimos encuentros de Inglaterra ha habido al menos un tanto tanto en la primera como en la segunda parte, exactamente el mismo registro que presenta España en sus cinco compromisos más recientes. La coincidencia entre ambas estadísticas deja un escenario equilibrado de cara a un partido que enfrenta a dos de las grandes selecciones europeas. 1XBET ofrece una cuota de 1.75 por que haya goles en ambas mitades y de 1.96 por que no se produzca este escenario.

articles.title: Brittany Mahomes Apologizes For Her Behavior During 'Sunday Night Football' Win
articles.summary: She said "a lot of bad words."
articles.body:
Brittany Mahomes was letting the expletives fly during Kansas City 's overtime win over the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday night.

The Chiefs topped the Colts, 33-30, in overtime in Week 2. Kansas City improved to 2-0 on the season with the win. It was a tightly-played game, and one that Brittany Mahomes got quite emotional over.

The wife of the Kansas City Chiefs quarterback admitted that she was heard saying "a lot of bad words" throughout her husband's second regular season game of the 2026 season. She posted an apology on social media.

"Sorry you had to hear me scream and say a lot of bad words for several hours," she wrote on her Instagram Story.

NFL games can be emotional, so fans will likely be accepting of this apology from Mrs. Mahomes.

We've all been there watching our favorite NFL team, right?

Patrick Mahomes warns teammates not to get complacent

While the Chiefs have started 2-0, there's still a long way to go this fall.

"I think more than anything [about] who we're playing is just staying hungry," Mahomes said this week, via transcript from the team. "In this league, it's week to week. One week they're patting you on your back, and one week they're telling you you're terrible. I think all offseason we heard about how bad we were, and guys were super hungry and came in with that mentality, and I think that's why we've had the success that we've had these first two weeks. And it's like, how can you keep that hunger? Now everybody's saying we're amazing and that we're great, and it's like we've got to keep the hunger that we've had this entire offseason.

"So that's what we're preaching, is like we're nowhere near where we want to be at. We're still so early in the season, and there's still so much for us to learn from and so much for us to get better at, and we have to have that mentality week in and week out if we want to go out there and have success."

Kansas City will take on Miami on Sunday.

articles.title: Max Verstappen reveals what really went wrong for Red Bull in Baku F1 qualifying
articles.summary: Verstappen says the internal combustion engine was not working properly during qualifying, which then led to further problems. The Red Bull driver adds that...
articles.body:
After setting the fastest time in final practice and feeling good about the upgrades, Verstappen hoped to pull off a surprise in Baku, but an engine problem threw a spanner in the works.

Initially, it appeared to be related to deployment issues and therefore problems on the electrical side of the power unit, but speaking to the (very small) group of Dutch media in the Baku paddock, Verstappen clarified what was actually going on.

"Throughout qualifying, already from Q1, I had a problem with the engine, which meant I was losing at least half a second compared to my team-mate. And it only got worse. In Q2 and Q3 it was a complete disaster, so I think we clearly have a problem with the engine."

When asked by Motorsport.com, Verstappen clarified that the problem was initially not about deployment – as it perhaps seemed – but rather the internal combustion engine.

"No, not on the electrical side. In Q1, we immediately saw a problem. Of course, at that point you still think, 'What could it be? Is the engine too cold or actually too hot?' All of that is possible, because it is all very sensitive nowadays. But later it became clear that we really did have a problem with the ICE. It only got worse and in Q3 that engine was no longer working properly at all."

How the initial issue led to further setbacks

That problem with the combustion engine subsequently caused numerous other issues, leaving Verstappen going from one problem to another on Friday afternoon.

"The top speed just became less and less. On that second lap in Q3, my battery wasn't charging either, but that was obviously because the combustion engine had a problem. That causes a lot of misfires and a lot of other problems, and it confuses the system completely."

The latter was clearly visible in the onboard footage. Between Turns 15 and 16, Verstappen's head suddenly jolted forward, whereas this would normally be a straightforward flat-out section.

"Yeah, because my battery switched off there", the Dutchman explained. "Because you're so slow on the straights, you obviously use more battery coming out of the corners to try to compensate for that. As a result, you go into super clipping in some places, and that clip is quite aggressive.

"The whole system was just confused. You spend longer on a straight because you're going slowly and as a result you use more battery. That's the same as what happens with Honda, you also see them clipping a lot more than everyone else because they have to spend longer at full throttle on the straights."

Besides the engine problems themselves, this also disrupted the run plan. Verstappen had to abort his second flying lap – or what should have been a flying lap – which in turn had consequences for the remainder of the session.

"I had to abort that lap, but then you lose so much tyre temperature, which is actually very important around here. You could see everyone pushing all the time and continuing to weave", Verstappen said, pointing out that almost everyone in Q3 completed just one long run – unlike in a normal Q3 session.

Only McLaren opted for a visit to the pitlane, but Verstappen continued: "You can see that it wasn't really a success for them either, so we just kept going.

"But if you have to abort a lap, then you don't have the right tyre temperature for the very last lap. And the engine is basically breaking down, and then there was a yellow flag on my final lap as well", he said, referring to the moment involving Lando Norris. "So I had to leave at least two tenths on the table in that corner."

An engine change, but no grid penalty for Verstappen?

Red Bull is currently investigating the engine problem further, but Verstappen's story makes it seem unlikely that he will start Saturday's race with the same ICE. However, the four-time world champion immediately makes clear that such an engine change will not result in a grid penalty.

"Well, if there are still question marks, we have to replace the engine. But we still have another engine available in the pool."

A grid penalty will follow later in the year, however, the Red Bull driver confirmed when asked by this website. "Yeah, there definitely has to be a penalty at some point."

In theory, Baku appeared to be quite a good place to take one, as overtaking seems possible, but Verstappen puts that into perspective.

"The problem is that everyone completely drains the battery on the long straight. So you can't really use the battery to overtake someone, because going from 100 to zero is the same for everyone."

It means Verstappen retains his eighth starting position and will still be aiming for the podium on Saturday, although he believes he could otherwise have started from the front row.

"It's obviously a real shame, because it had been going well this week. Maybe I wouldn't have matched George's time, but there's such a big gap between P1 and P2, we definitely would have been somewhere in between."

articles.title: Fantasy Football Week 3 Fades & Busts: Hard to trust big-name Bears on MNF
articles.summary: Matt Okada takes you through the players he's avoiding in Week 3 for fantasy football.
articles.body:
Welcome to the third of 17 weekly articles spotlighting the fantasy fades of the week! I am your host, Matt Okada, and I'll be bringing you half a dozen potential busts each and every Friday, from now until fantasy championships.

While I don't toot my own horn often, if you're new to this series, here's how last week's six picks performed:

Justin Herbert vs. LV: 9.88 points (QB24)

Quinshon Judkins at TB: 7.3 points (RB32)

Jeremiyah Love vs. SEA: 6.0 points (RB38)

Kyle Pitts Sr. vs. CAR: 2.0 points (TE38)

As a note, just because a player earns a "fade" or "bust" designation doesn't automatically mean they should be benched — it depends on the rest of your roster or the options on your waiver wire. But you can expect them to fall short of expectations (when I get them right). I include a "What to Do" section for every player to help with that.

Without further ado, here is my list for Week 3 of the 2026 season.

I could take the "easy" calls this week — like Daniel Jones versus Houston or Baker Mayfield versus Minnesota — but that's not the point of this column. Instead, my "Fade of the Week" at quarterback is last year's QB2 overall, Drake Maye.

Unfortunately, Maye has not looked good through two weeks. We made a lot of noise about his poor arsenal of pass-catchers last year, but with A.J. Brown sidelined, Stefon Diggs and Kayshon Boutte sound magnificent right now. Their absence has seriously hurt Maye's fantasy output, especially downfield (throws of 10+ air yards). Last year, he scored the second-most fantasy points on downfield passes, with an elite 0.73 EPA/dropback. Through two weeks, he has -0.2 fantasy points and a -0.21 EPA/dropback on those same throws.

And while I fully expect Maye to bounce back in 2026 (perhaps when Brown returns), I don't see it happening this week on the road in Jacksonville . The Jags held each of Bo Nix and Deshaun Watson to 14 fantasy points, and while Maye is better in principle than both those guys, he has not been better in reality (so far). Plus, while this game might sound explosive on paper, the Patriots only have an implied total of 21.25 points, below the median this week.

What to do ❓ Maye is outside my top 12 this week, behind typical fantasy backups and potential waiver-wire streamers like Drew Lock , Bryce Young and Tyler Shough . Despite where you probably drafted him, you can legitimately bench the Patriots QB for this Sunday.

Travis Etienne Jr. , RB, Saints vs. Raiders

After two games, Travis Etienne Jr.'s four-year, $48 million contract with New Orleans seems ... misplaced. Between Kendre Miller playing significant snaps in Week 1, Alvin Kamara picking up those snaps in Week 2 and undrafted rookie CJ Donaldson seeing bafflingly heavy usage in both games, Etienne has handled just 51.5% of the running back snaps. Even more concerning, he has shouldered just 49.1% of the running back opportunities. That's certainly not RB1 volume ... and it's probably not even RB2 volume. While Etienne saw nine targets in Week 1 with Kamara inactive, he was out-targeted six-to-two by Kamara in his Week 2 return. And counting only rushing yards and rushing touchdowns, Etienne has scored just 7.1 fantasy points through Week 2 ... 41st among running backs.

Now, he takes on a surprising Raiders defense that's allowed -0.39 EPA per carry so far in 2026, the best mark in the entire NFL. We may not see Vegas' true colors until its upcoming stretch against the Chiefs, Patriots, Bills and Rams (yikes), but the Raiders have a refreshed roster and it's looked dangerous against the Dolphins and Chargers. Either way, Etienne isn't seeing the usage we need from our fantasy starters and might be a fade regardless of matchup.

What to do ❓ Etienne is outside the top 24 at running back and might only be viable as a low-end FLEX in PPR leagues this week. Don't be surprised to see another single-digit outing from the Saints' supposed lead running back.

Bhayshul Tuten , RB, Jaguars vs. Patriots

This might draw the ire of all the Tuten-touters in the fantasy community, but I'm still not convinced about the explosive Jaguars running back. Yes, he looks incredibly fast every time he touches the ball, certainly faster than backfield mate Chris Rodriguez Jr. Despite that, he's only seen 49.1% of the running back snaps through two games, with Ameer Abdullah and LeQuint Allen Jr. also seeing some usage. Moreover, if we narrow in on the "green zone" — the opposing 10-yard line and in — Tuten has taken three of seven RB snaps and two of five RB touches for Jacksonville. And, finally, he has not flashed any upside as a receiver, with just three targets, resulting in 19 yards, across two contests.

Sometime soon, Tuten is very likely to bust out a 100-yard, 20-fantasy-point performance. But it's not coming against the New England Patriots this Sunday. The Pats defense has allowed the fifth-lowest rushing success rate (33.3%) and has not surrendered double-digit fantasy points to a single running back so far this season. While you can argue that's a reflection of the committee backfields they've faced — the Steelers and the Seahawks — that same logic should be applied to the Jags, based on the usage we've seen so far. Tuten has a lot of upside but a very concerning floor.

What to do ❓ Like Etienne, Tuten is outside my top 24 at running back. He is a bit better as a FLEX, simply considering Jacksonville's implied total, but he's a risky one I'd avoid for someone like Quinshon Judkins or Josh Downs .

I am currently ice-cold on Rome Odunze. And I don't mean he's a cool play ... I mean I have zero interest in starting him this week. Through two games, despite running the most routes by a Chicago wide receiver (57), Odunze has seen a 12.3% target share, well below Luther Burden III and 32-year-old Kalif Raymond (both over 20%). And while he has totaled 95 yards on five catches, that includes two catches for 62 yards on plays where Caleb Williams bought an extended amount of time before the throw (as only he and a couple of other QBs can).

Heading into Week 3 against the Eagles, the Bears will almost certainly be down to second-string QB Tyson Bagent , if he clears the concussion protocol , or third-string QB Case Keenum if Bagent can't. Neither of those guys has the elusiveness, or the scrambling prowess, or the arm ... or really anything at the level that Williams does.

And to make matters much worse in Week 3, Odunze will be taking on Quinyon Mitchell , Riq Woolen and a tough Eagles secondary. Philly has allowed just nine catches and no touchdowns to outside wide receivers this year, and Mitchell and Woolen have combined to allow just 3.4 yards per target and a -17.3% completion rate over expected. We benched Carnell Tate against this same secondary last week, with excellent results. Like Tuten, Odunze will have some big games this year, but you should not expect one this week.

What to do ❓ As I mentioned at the top, Odunze is miles outside my lineup-relevant rankings. He shouldn't even be a FLEX consideration in most leagues, and I'd play guys like Denzel Boston, Devaughn Vele , Dontayvion Wicks and Adonai Mitchell over him.

Terry McLaurin , WR, Commanders vs. Seahawks

This is Terry McLaurin's second appearance in this column in three weeks. Not an auspicious start to the year for the former WR1 in Washington. And yes, I said "former" WR1, because I truly believe Stefon Diggs has taken that job (for now). Despite the fact that McLaurin has run quite a few more routes (68, most on the team), Diggs has a higher target share (23.8% to McLaurin's 20.6%). And if you look at target rate — the frequency with which a player is targeted when they're running a route — McLaurin is actually fifth on his own team, behind Diggs, tight end John Bates , rookie Antonio Williams and running back Rachaad White . McLaurin is averaging just 0.9 yards per route run and has seen just two red-zone targets ... resulting in one catch for six yards and one interception.

In Week 3, it gets uglier, as McLaurin takes on the Seahawks secondary. Devon Witherspoon , Josh Jobe and Co. have been a disaster for outside wide receivers, allowing the fourth-fewest yards per target (5.4) and third-lowest passer rating when targeted (28.9) to wideouts actually aligned out wide. On the whole, they've allowed just 10.3 fantasy points per game and 0.69 points per target to all wide receivers, both fewest in the league. Oh, and Washington will be playing backup quarterback Marcus Mariota , with Jayden Daniels sidelined. It's all red flags for McLaurin this week.

What to do ❓ McLaurin is frankly not much higher than Odunze in my rankings, and you can implement essentially the same approach with both this weekend.

Ugh. Based on draft capital, expectations and position, I think it's fair to say Colston Loveland has been the biggest bust in fantasy through two games. Now, that's a very small sample size, so we're not jettisoning him from our rosters just yet. But we have to be legitimately concerned. Loveland has seen an abysmal 8.8% target share in Chicago, 31st among tight ends, lower than such household names (sarcasm) as Greg Dulcich , Tommy Tremble and Josh Oliver . Over the last decade , his 0.05 yards per route run on 61 routes is the worst through the first two weeks of a season by any player with 50+ routes run, behind guys like Donte Moncrief , Braxton Miller , Ryan Griffin and Ian Thomas.

And, like Odunze earlier, Loveland will be down to a backup quarterback against an extremely tough defense. The Eagles have also crushed tight ends this season: their 7.2 fantasy points allowed to the position is second-fewest (behind the Niners) and their 0.80 points per target allowed is fourth-fewest. Granted, the Eagles have played the Titans and Commanders, but we haven't seen anything from Loveland this season that suggests he'll suddenly break that trend in Week 3. Even at a very shallow position, after drafting him in the early rounds, Loveland is a terrible play on Monday night.

What to do ❓ If you can bench Loveland for another tight end you drafted as a backup or picked up off waivers — someone like Dalton Kincaid (who's been a revelation), Dalton Schultz (big year for Daltons), Isaiah Likely , Juwan Johnson or maybe even Pat Freiermuth (in a brilliant matchup) — do it this week.

articles.title: Bold Fantasy Football Predictions for Week 3
articles.summary: The Yahoo Fantasy football crew gets bold for Week 3
articles.body:
The Yahoo Fantasy Football crew is ready to get bold for Week 3. Which one of these predictions will come true?

We have a solid total of 47.5 brewing in the upcoming Jets-Lions matchup this weekend. Of course, Detroit is doing the heavy lifting on that one, but don't discount the Jets' ability to at least engage in a shootout in this matchup. The Jets offense is 10th in dropback EPA and top 10 in time of possession per drive so far this season. They've been able to hang onto the ball and mount drives successfully with Geno Smith under center. I firmly believe this offense is not going to be a joke this season.

Adonai Mitchell is a beneficiary. He's a full-time player for this team, as he's run a route on 83% of the dropbacks. He's also currently leading the team in targets by one, with 15 to 14 for Garrett Wilson . Mitchell has also been efficient with his looks, leading the team in first downs per route run. There will always be some volatility with Mitchell as a player, but you can chase the ceiling this week in a high-scoring script against a Lions defense that can't cover anyone on the backend. — Matt Harmon

Tetairoa McMillan gives us his first WR1 finish

Doubting Bryce Young 's fantasy relevance made sense before this season, but two games into this version of him, that skepticism doesn't hold up. When under duress, his numbers haven't looked better. But with EPA per dropback and success rate numbers inside the top 12, Young looks like he's taken the step forward we've wanted for him.

Tetairoa McMillan is the direct beneficiary — he's soaking up more than 40% of Young's targets on pressured snaps, and his target rate and air-yard share both sit comfortably inside true WR1 range. Facing Cleveland is what turns the opportunity into a top-12 finish. Their defense ranks 22nd in yards allowed to outside receivers, 19th in EPA allowed per play, and 22nd in success rate allowed. Jacksonville already exploited that perimeter in their season opener with Parker Washington and Brian Thomas Jr. , and Tampa Bay tried the same blueprint the following week.

McMillan isn't just comparable to that archetype — he's the better route runner. And with that type of environment, this is the week his name finally shows up near the top of the box score. — Chris Allen

Terrance Ferguson finishes as a top-five fantasy TE in Week 3

With Sean McVay admitting Puka Nacua isn't making great progress in his recovery from a hip/groin injury, the Rams are going to need their other playmakers to step up once again. Last week, Davante Adams took a time machine back five years and turned in a vintage performance, catching all 10 of his targets for 195 yards and two touchdowns. That overshadowed an impressive outing from Ferguson, who finished with six receptions, 54 yards and a score. Ferguson's nine targets were seven more than the next closest player in the Rams offense.

This shouldn't surprise anyone either. The team spoke all offseason about increasing the young tight end's role and their lack of a proven No. 3 wideout positioned him to be a real threat in the passing game. Nacua's injury only increased that involvement. Ferguson scored three touchdowns as a rookie and all three occurred when either Puka or Adams were sidelined. Until Nacua returns, Ferguson will be what fantasy managers thought they were getting in Colston Loveland — and he's still available on the waiver wire in 77% of Yahoo leagues. — Justin Boone

Josh Downs goes for 100 yards and a touchdown against Houston

Downs' role was already trending in the right direction, and with Alec Pierce on IR, Indianapolis is going to have to lean on Downs even more in both two- and three-wide receiver sets. Through two games, Houston has allowed 369 receiving yards to wide receivers on 39 targets, with opposing WR rooms averaging 43 PPR points per game. This secondary has given fantasy managers plenty to attack, and now Downs gets an expanded role in exactly the type of matchup I want to target.

I have him ranked significantly higher than consensus this week because I think the opportunity is about to take another step forward. He's no longer just a slot receiver we hope gets enough targets. The Colts need him on the field and involved. My bold prediction: Downs clears 100 receiving yards, scores a touchdown and finishes Week 3 as a top-12 fantasy wide receiver. — Ray Garvin

The Eagles chose Wicks in free agency and it's paid off so far. Although he's only had 10 targets, you don't need much volume in this passing offense to produce. Chicago 's secondary is banged up and vulnerable, only ranking above average versus fantasy receivers so far because of the downpour in Week 2. With Chicago playing a healthy amount of man coverage, it sets both Jalen Hurts and Wicks up for big-play opportunities down the field. If DeVonta Smith or Saquon Barkley are sidelined, the chances only improve. — Joel Smyth

It didn't help the Texans much — they scored just six points against Cincinnati — but Dalton Schultz was super in the Week 2 loss (12-140-0, 14 targets) while none of the Houston receivers could get traction. It could be argued that the Bengals were partners in the Schultz spike game, focusing on downfield targets and willing to concede the shorter stuff over the middle.

Looking ahead to Week 3, not much has changed for Houston; Nico Collins is likely out again, the receivers look like speculation plays at best and Indy's seam coverage has been weak for two weeks. Put Schultz down for 80 or more yards again. — Scott Pianowski

Quinshon Judkins finishes as a top-10 RB

Judkins enters Week 3 with the lowest success rate of any RB in the NFL. He only managed 21 yards on 12 carries last time out. So why am I optimistic about Week 3? Simple: the Panthers run defense is not the Bucs or Jaguars. Carolina currently allows the highest yards per carry in the NFL (6.3 per attempt) and will be without Devin Lloyd , meaning the Panthers will be starting two linebackers who were not on the roster a month ago. Todd Monken will not want to put the ball in Deshaun Watson 's hands for this game. An early turnover could quickly turn the crowd against his quarterback. Instead, look for the Browns to lean into Judkins and for the second-year back to show the same flash as he did as a rookie — with the Panthers already missing 24 tackles as a defensive unit in two games. — Josh Norris

articles.title: Asian Games 2026: Gulveer Singh headlines India's athletics surge
articles.summary: Moments after finishing his 10,000m race, Gulveer Singh went down on his knees.
articles.body: Moments after finishing his 10,000m race, Gulveer Singh went down on his knees. He touched the ground, then fell on his back and briefly looked up at the sky. When he got up he flashed a smile, which was probably brighter than the silver he had just won. From the bronze from Hangzhou, the upgrade was deserving. The medal was probably loading since June 28, when he won India’s maiden 10,000m at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.At the Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium on Friday night, Gulveer came home in 28:29.38 minutes to finish between two African-born Bahrain citizens. While Birhanu Balew clinched gold with a time of 28:27.51 minutes, Albert Kipto ended third in 28:34.18.Gulveer, the 28-year-old from Atrauli was tactically sharp and focused on not falling behind. By the fifth lap, he was third in a leader pack of six athletes. He rarely fell behind, barring the midrace when he briefly occupied the fifth position. With four laps to go, the Naib Subedar in the Army upped the pace and moved to second position. By that time the front runners had left behind the rest of the field, with the sixth-placed runner almost 150m behind.When the bell to signal the last lap was rang, it felt like it kicked an adrenaline rush in the eventual podium finishers, with the final 200m more like a sprint race with Balew in top gear. An elated Gulveer later said, “It feels good to win a silver for India at the Asian Games. It is very satisfying.”Gulveer, who like most of the other distance runners trains in Colorado Springs, said, “Races such as these are different from races where you’re chasing time. I trusted the race plan of the coaches, which was to stay relaxed, remain with the lead group, and make my move at the right moment.”Baranica Elangovan suffered a career threatening injury in 2019 and it took her a couple years to find her way back. She raised the bar gradually, until she became the first woman pole vaulter to clinch a medal at the competition. A late bloomer who switched from long jump and triple jump on the insistence of her coach Milber Bertrand Russell, cleared 4.15 metres on her fifth attempt to take the bronze, while the gold stayed at home with Misaki Morota’s personal best of 4.55, earning her the top spot. Chunge Niu (4.50m) of China was secondOn a milestone medal, the 29-year-old said, “It’s always been my dream to rewrite history and I’ve done that today. That said, I’m really happy that I could win a medal for the country.” Such was Baranica’s focus that she didn’t realise she had won a medal until her compatriot Sindhushree Ganesh, who ended last with no mark, told her.“When Sindhu told me, I didn’t believe her. I checked, re-checked and checked again. Only then did I believe the medal was mine. When I saw the medal icon against my name, I signalled to my coach Russell in the stands to check again,” said the athlete, who hails from a farmer’s family in Kuthalam in Tamil Nadu.From the ignominy of a four-year dope ban to standing on the podium at the continental event, Manpreet Kaur’s life has come full circle. Watched by her teenage daughter, the shot putter with a fourth attempt throw of 17.17 metres won bronze behind the Chinese duo of Song Jiayuan (19.40m) and Zhang Linru (18.14m), who won gold and silver, respectively. Manpreet, who returned from the ban in 2021, was slow off the mark with a 16.32, while he best came in her penultimate attempt. The other Indian in the fray, Krishna Jayasankar Menon, finished fifth with a best effort of 16.57m.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: D Gukesh ‘tricks’ Germany, keeps Indian challenge alive at Chess Olympiad
articles.summary: Gukesh spooked Alexander Donchenko, helping India score a seemingly unlikely victory over overnight joint leaders Germany in the ninth round of the Chess
articles.body: Gukesh spooked Alexander Donchenko, helping India score a seemingly unlikely victory over overnight joint leaders Germany in the ninth round of the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand on Friday.The win helped India move to 15 match-points, one behind leaders and hosts Uzbekistan (16), who humbled USA. Nodirbek Yakubboev scored another crucial win for the hosts, this time over Hans Niemann. Uzbekistan’s second-strength team and Armenia are also level with India on points with just two rounds remaining.India women (15 points) humbled Uzbekistan 3-1 but are still trailing China (17) by two match-points. China, who have not fielded their full-strength team, continued their march towards the gold medal with a win over Armenia, in which Zhu Jiner and Lu Miaoyi scored full points.The draw between Kazakhstan and Mongolia (15 each) also helped India, as neither could overtake them. Divya Deshmukh and Vanitka Agrawal, individual gold medallists in the last Olympiad, scripted the success of the Indian women as they defeated lower-rated opponents.B Savitha Shri’s stunning sequence of seven successive wins came to an end with a draw against Guildona Karimova (Elo 2242), while K Humpy held her own on the top board.World champion Gukesh once again showed why he is such a dangerous rival. Germany, somewhat surprisingly, decided to rest Rasmus Svane, who had two successive wins in the preceding rounds, and chose to field Donchenko against Gukesh.The 28-year-old German almost justified the faith shown in him by pushing Gukesh to a corner. However, he then gave too much importance to Gukesh’s h-pawn and misplaced his pieces.ALSO READ: 'Not too much pressure': How Zhu Jiner turned struggles in India into taking China closer to Chess Olympiad gold | ExclusiveWhile this drama was unfolding, Nihal Sarin had already drawn his game against Frederik Svane despite flirting with danger and mental abyss. R Praggnanandhaa and Erigaisi Arjun were unable to break through the defences of Vincent Keymer and Matthias Blubaum respectively.Arjun had even sacrificed his knight but reached a queen-and-extra-pawns versus queen, bishop-and-pawns endgame. However, with Gukesh turning the tables, the draws by Arjun and Praggnanandhaa were no longer a losing cause.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Asian Games 2026: Joshna Chinappa, Velavan Senthilkumar settle for bronze in Squash mixed doubles
articles.summary: India’s Joshna Chinappa and Velavan Senthilkumar came agonisingly close to a place in the Asian Games mixed doubles final, losing a dramatic semifinal to
articles.body: India’s Joshna Chinappa and Velavan Senthilkumar came agonisingly close to a place in the Asian Games mixed doubles final, losing a dramatic semifinal to Hong Kong’s Tang Ming Hong and Lee Ka Yi 1-2 (10-11, 11-2, 11-10).The Indian pair looked to have one foot in the final after fighting back from a tight opening-game defeat and dominating the second. They then led 9-7 in the decider and had three match points, only for the Hong Kong pair to stage a stunning comeback and snatch the contest in a nerve-wracking finish.The defeat meant Joshna and Velavan had to settle for a bronze medal.India lose first game by narrowest marginThe opening game was a tense battle with neither pair able to establish a significant advantage. Joshna and Velavan edged ahead at one stage, but Tang and Lee responded with three straight points to move 9-8 ahead. The Indians quickly levelled at 9-9 before Hong Kong earned game point.India fought back again to make it 10-10, but Tang and Lee won the next point to take the game 11-10 and move within one game of the final.Joshna, Velavan hit back in styleThe Indians responded emphatically in the second game. Joshna and Velavan came out aggressively, looking to finish points quickly rather than getting drawn into the long rallies that had characterised the opening game.They raced into a 3-0 lead and extended it to 7-2. From there, they did not give Hong Kong another point, closing out the game 11-2 to force a decider. Three match points slip away in dramatic deciderThe deciding game produced the most intense action of the contest. Joshna and Velavan initially trailed 2-5 but fought back to make it 4-5. The game then turned into a battle of attrition, with long rallies and several 'lets', where a point is replayed because of an obstruction, adding to the tension.The Indians eventually levelled at 6-6 before taking control. They moved 8-7 ahead and then stretched their lead to 9-7, with Velavan producing some outstanding defensive work. At 9-7, India had three match points but could not convert them. Tang and Lee held their nerve to win the next three points and level the game at 10-10.The next rally was fiercely contested and ended in controversy. India initially appeared to have won the point, with Velavan briefly celebrating, but the point was disallowed. Hong Kong then won the following point to complete a remarkable 11-10 comeback and book their place in the final.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.body: India beat Iran 37-33 to clinch the gold medal in the women's kabaddi event at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Saturday, adding another gold to the country's medal tally.The victory marks India's fourth gold medal in women's kabaddi at the Asian Games. The Indian team had previously won gold in 2010, 2014 and 2022, while finishing runners-up in 2018.India entered the final as defending champions after beating Chinese Taipei 26-25 in the gold-medal match at the Hangzhou Games.The gold also adds to a productive morning for India on September 26. articles.title: Carolina Navarro: "Dejar fuera a Alejandra Salazar ha sido muy duro a nivel emocional"
articles.standfirst: La seleccionadora española de pádel atiende a MARCA poco después de ofrecer su convocatoria
articles.summary: La seleccionadora española de pádel atiende a MARCA poco después de ofrecer su convocatoria
articles.body: Carolina Navarro Björk (Málaga, 1976), una leyenda del pádel mundial, ha vivido una semana de lo más especial. Este jueves, en Madrid, hizo pública la lista de las ocho jugadoras que buscarán la décima corona mundial femenina desde el próximo 2 de noviembre en Doha (Qatar). Sobre la confección de la lista, la gran decisión de dejar fuera a Alejandra Salazar, la convocatoria de Marta Ortega, la irrupción de las jóvenes Martina Calvo y Andrea Ustero y mucho más, ha hablado con MARCA Pádel minutos después del anuncio. Pregunta. ¿Qué has sentido cuando se ha hecho público, a través de ese vídeo superchulo, esta convocatoria de ocho elegidas para el Mundial? Respuesta. Pues no sé si la palabra es alivio o tranquilidad, porque la verdad es que llevo unos meses bastante complicados con el tema de la convocatoria. Realmente ha sido una decisión muy difícil por todo lo que conllevaba y por la cantidad de jugadoras tan buenas que tenemos. Pero bueno, estoy tranquila porque, al final, creo que he elegido a las jugadoras para tener el mejor equipo posible. P. ¿Por qué estas ocho? R. Pienso que las seis primeras, básicamente por ranking y por juego, eran totalmente indiscutibles. Y las otras dos jugadoras estaban entre, por un lado, Tamara y Martina. Tamara lo está haciendo muy bien, pero realmente Martina está con una actitud en pista que es tremenda, jugando muy bien y cerrando muy bien los partidos. Es una jugadora agresiva también y, al final, en las condiciones de Doha, con calor y una pista rápida, creo que puede aportar mucho al equipo. Y luego, por otro lado, estaba la decisión entre Martita y Alejandra, que ha sido muy complicada porque, evidentemente, Alejandra se lo merece por toda la trayectoria que lleva. Estaba jugando bien y habría sido su último Mundial. Pero también para Martita podía haber sido, o puede ser, su último Mundial. Creo que está rindiendo muy bien, es una jugadora muy rápida, que también tiene sus momentos de agresividad, y creo que, al final, está rindiendo mejor. Como te digo, he tratado de borrar un poco todo el ruido que tenía alrededor y pensar de la forma más objetiva posible cuál podría ser el mejor equipo, sin pensar en quién es suplente o quién no, ni quiénes son rivales porque, al final, cualquiera de las ocho puede jugar si hay lesiones. Así que ha sido una decisión de equipo y estoy muy contenta y a muerte con ellas. P. ¿Cuándo cerraste el equipo y entregaste la lista? R. Bueno, la Federación no sabía nada. Ha sido todo un poco extraño porque, con el tema de la rueda de prensa, no quería que se filtrara nada. Ni Juanjo ni yo queríamos darle la lista a nadie. La única persona que lo sabía era la que necesitábamos para hacer el vídeo. De hecho, en el Mundial de Veteranos nos estaban llamando para saber la lista y poder hacer el vídeo, y ahí se la dimos. Yo le di siete nombres. Juanjo le había dado su lista hacía tiempo y la última jugadora se la di hace dos días, básicamente porque no quería que se filtrara. Entonces éramos tres los que lo sabíamos. La Federación se ha enterado en directo. Las jugadoras que estaban dentro de la selección se han enterado en directo y a las que no iban se lo comuniqué justo antes de empezar la gala. P. ¿Cómo te has sentido? Al final hay un componente que va más allá del plano puramente deportivo. Está el componente emocional por lo que supone, en este caso, que Alejandra Salazar no juegue el que hubiese sido su último Mundial. R. Básicamente porque soy una persona con bastante empatía y yo he pasado por su lugar. He estado en esa situación, disputando mi último Mundial y sin saber si jugaba o no. En su momento no jugué y fue muy duro. Y, yo sé que, al final, con Alejandra, la verdad es que me llevo fenomenal. La conozco, hemos jugado juntas, y la verdad es que era una decisión muy dura a nivel personal y emocional. Pero la realidad de todo esto es que también puede ser el de Martita, como te he dicho antes. A nivel emocional es complicado, pero al final tengo que tratar de sacar toda la parte subjetiva y ser lo más objetiva posible, pensar con cabeza. Al final es lo que ha salido, que es lo que yo quería, y esperemos que pueda ir muy bien y que sea un equipazo. P. Ponemos mucho el foco en Alejandra, y eso es lógico por la figura que es, además de que es su último año. Pero ¿por qué te llevas a Marta Ortega? R. También lleva muchos años representando a la selección. Es una grandísima jugadora y me la llevo básicamente porque está rindiendo muy bien. Es una jugadora rápida y creo que las condiciones de Doha son buenas para que ella también rinda bien. Se lo ha merecido y se lo ha ganado en la pista. P. Hay dos grandes novedades, que son Martina Calvo y Andrea. ¿Cómo ves a estas jóvenes generaciones que, con Claudia, parecía que ya lo habíamos visto todo a nivel de precocidad... R. Es una locura. Las jugadoras que tenemos son muy jóvenes. Yo no sé si es el equipo más joven de los que llevamos y hay un relevo generacional importante. Gemma es la veterana y solo tiene 34 años. P. Es tremendo, realmente. R. El resto son jugadoras muy jóvenes, pero con mucha experiencia: se han metido en finales, han ganado partidos y están compitiendo muy bien, así que por ello estoy tranquila. Es cierto que ponerse la camiseta de España no es lo mismo que jugar Premier Padel, pero creo que todas son increíbles y lo harán fenomenal. P. ¿Tiene España el mejor equipo? R. Sí. P. ¿Es favorita? R. Sí. P. ¿Tienes en la cabeza una idea de las tres parejas que formarían en la final? R. Sí, pero no te lo voy a decir (risas), aunque sí que es cierto que llevamos el mejor equipo, claramente. Pero luego hay que ver cómo se gestionan las emociones de llevar la camiseta y cuánto pesa. En el caso, por ejemplo, de Argentina, cuando se ponen la camiseta juegan diez veces más. Entonces, bueno, yo creo que estas chicas lo van a hacer muy bien. P. Hablando de Argentina, ¿cómo las ves? Porque es verdad que, con el paso de los años, sobre todo en la última década, da la sensación de que se ha ido agrandando más esa diferencia de nivel entre ambas selecciones. R. Sí. Bueno, ahora tienen tres jugadoras muy buenas: Claudia, Aranza y Delfi. Tienen otras jugadoras que también juegan muy bien. Ellas van a ir a ganar, con la camiseta puesta, gritando y dándolo todo. Entonces, si de repente uno de esos dos primeros puntos se te escapa, puede complicarse el título. Pero creo que llevamos un grandísimo equipo que lo va a hacer muy bien y ojalá podamos llevarnos el título para casa. P. ¿Qué selección ves que puede estar acercándose un poquito al nivel de Argentina? R. Creo que Italia, Francia y Portugal tienen muy buenos equipos.

articles.title: Jay Meena battled typhoid, hip injury and self-doubt to win historic Asian Games medal
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Weeks before the 2026 Asian Games, Jay Meena was bedridden with typhoid and a severe infection, losing eight kilograms in the process.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Weeks before the 2026 Asian Games, Jay Meena was bedridden with typhoid and a severe infection, losing eight kilograms in the process. Sent home to Dewas in Madhya Pradesh from an Asian Games training camp in Srinagar in August, the 25-year-old needed his parents to feed him by hand for nearly a week.Recovery was difficult too. For a week, he would feel dizzy after walking just a few steps. An iffy stomach only made his attempts to regain his strength and return to shape more challenging.Cut to the present. The moment his opponent’s final shot drifted long and Meena won India’s first-ever Asian Games medal in Soft Tennis, the 25-year-old collapsed onto the baseline in joy. Moments later, he was back on his feet, arms spread wide and roaring towards the Indian bench. The celebration marked far more than a bronze medal. It was a historic moment for Indian Soft Tennis, with Meena securing the country’s first-ever Asian Games medal in the sport.Meena narrates that for 15 days, he was completely out of action and the clock on the Asian Games was ticking down. All his efforts over the course of the past few months had just been undone by the viral infection. “I started light warm-ups, I started training again. I could not sit at home at such a moment,” he tells TimesofIndia.com, with the urgency of the situation still quite evident in his voice.He recovered just in time to board the flight to Tokyo and the Shinkansen (train) to Nagoya. The ordeal, however, was far from over.Recovering from typhoid meant nutrition became almost as important as training. But in Nagoya, the predominantly seafood menu offered few vegetarian options. In the absence of a traditional Games village, he made do with corn, bread, butter, milk and cereal. While urging the authorities to send a chef alongside future contingents, Meena stressed that pre-packaged foods cannot replace fresh preparations.The lingering effects of the illness surfaced during his semi-final loss to Japan’s Takuya Kurosaka (2-4), as Meena required a medical timeout to continue the closely contested match at the Higashiyama Park Tennis Center.He later revealed that a hip niggle was preventing him from playing his backhand, with a “pinching” pain each time he went for the shot.Then there is the obvious mental challenge of representing the country at such a competition. Little by little, the chances of winning a medal got smaller and the internal battles got bigger. First, the men’s team, also featuring Meena, lost 0-2 to Indonesia in the quarter-finals. Then, Meena and Aadhya Tiwari lost in the first round of mixed doubles.“There were a lot of disappointing nights, a lot of self-doubts that we had all night. When we lost the quarter-final against Indonesia, it was a big opportunity on the 18th. If we had won that day, then Soft Tennis would have opened the (medal) account for India. After that, there was (the) mixed doubles in which Aadhya and I reached the pre-quarter-finals but lost. So, there were very disappointing nights going on day by day,” said Meena in reflection of the start of the competition.“After all these things, it was very difficult to come back and gain confidence after the self-doubt. It was very difficult to wake up every morning with new hope and get on the court with a new zeal,” he continued.A career that almost wasn't and brother's sacrificeThe desperate need for belief and confidence is not new to Meena’s career. When he was in Class 10 and his foray into Soft Tennis was not going anywhere, Rameshwar, his lawyer father, suggested stepping away and focusing elsewhere. It was then that his mother stepped in and pushed for a rethink and patience. That punt paid off.Years later, Meena began rewriting Indian Soft Tennis history, winning National Games gold, India’s first World Championships medal in mixed doubles, and a breakthrough Asian Championships bronze.Still one of his biggest supporters, Meena’s father travelled with his son to national tournaments and even accompanied him to Japan for the Asian Games.The financial condition was not so good. We had to force him to stay back because my father could not afford more than what was costing me to play. That’s why my brother went into Engineering.The hardest sacrifice, perhaps, belongs to someone else: his younger brother Yash.Two years younger than Jay, Yash was a Soft Tennis player and national medallist. But with their financial condition less than ideal, a hard decision was needed and Jay’s career continued.“The financial condition was not so good. We had to force him to stay back because my father could not afford more than what was costing me to play. That’s why he went into Engineering,” says the MP native.“Somewhere or the other, my younger brother’s life was sacrificed because of me. Because my parents paid more attention to me for about 10 years. If we had continued, then maybe he would have been with me in the Asian Games,” he continued. From gully cricket to Soft Tennis courtsJay Meena was like many other youngsters in the country who harboured cricket ambitions. He would play gully cricket with other kids in his street. The notorious boy in him, though, tended to pick up fights and get into altercations. Even at school, he would bother the teachers, including once setting off fireworks under his principal’s desk.The situation came to a head when he was rusticated from Ebenazer Higher Secondary School in the fourth grade. With no school willing to take him in, Pioneer Public School agreed, but on one condition: that he join the sports academy. With his parents keen on keeping Jay’s antics in check, they agreed to sports coach Sudesh Sangte’s condition.Sangte, a former national-level Kho Kho player and now the national Soft Tennis coach, had set up a two-court facility.“My family was very upset with me. I would not stay at home, I would not allow anyone to relax. I used to fight. Their parents used to complain a lot and my family threw me out. They said, you are out now. You stay on the ground [academy]. Don’t come home in the morning and evening. Come home at night,” Jay says with a laugh.“The school teachers and my classmates were (also) upset. I was rusticated in the fourth grade. And no other school was admitting me. At that time, Mr. Sudesh Sangte, who is my head coach now, he got me admitted. I took admission during the summer holidays.”“They had made two courts in their school. So, I was playing in their academy during the summer holidays. I didn’t even know, when I started playing for India and now won the Asian Games medal,” he explained.For me, this is an Olympic medal. It’s no less than an Olympic medal. All the strongest teams come in the Asian contingent. So this feels like an Olympic medal to me because Soft Tennis is not part of the OlympicsBigger than an Asian Games medalEven though the International Soft Tennis Federation (ISTF) has 65 members, including Eritrea, Basque Country, Curacao, Malta, North Korea and Uganda, the sport is dominated by Asian countries. At the last World Soft Tennis Championships, held in Anseong, South Korea, in 2024, six countries had picked up medals: Korea, Japan, Chinese Taipei, China, India and the Philippines.At the 2026 Asian Games, there were entries from 13 National Olympic Committees (NOCs), with Cambodia, Japan, South Korea, Mongolia, the Philippines and North Korea sending the maximum permissible 10 players. In the end, athletes from Japan, Chinese Taipei, North Korea, South Korea, Indonesia, India and the Philippines walked away with medals.Considering the dominance of Asian countries in Soft Tennis, Jay weighs this new medal on an Olympic scale.“For me, this is an Olympic medal. It’s no less than an Olympic medal. All the strongest teams come in the Asian contingent. So this feels like an Olympic medal to me because Soft Tennis is not part of the Olympics,” the youngster explained.Sixteen years ago, Soft Tennis was simply a way to keep an unruly fourth-grader out of trouble. Today, it has given India a historic Asian Games medal.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Yuki Kurihara, Japan’s 11-year-old e-sports prodigy, wins Asian Games gold
articles.summary: Gold medallist Yuki Kurihara, a primary school student, is youngest athlete in host country Japan’s Asian Games history.
articles.body:
Japan’s 11-year-old e-sports prodigy Yuki Kurihara said he was “embarrassed” after winning Asian Games gold on Saturday by thrashing a series of opponents up to three times his age.

The bespectacled primary school student, believed to be the youngest competitor at the games in Aichi-Nagoya , won the Puyo Puyo Champions final 10-2.

He is the youngest athlete in the host country Japan’s Asian Games history.

Puyo Puyo Champions is a puzzle game where players try to clear their screen of coloured blobs by lining them up and popping them.

Looking unruffled throughout, Kurihara waltzed into the gold medal match with a string of dazzling displays.

He crushed Thailand’s Tanarak Wongkitkun – a relative veteran at 28 – 10-1 in the semifinals to ensure at least a silver medal.

He did not even smile after beating South Korea’s 24-year-old Kang Dongshin in the final, having gone down 1-0 early on.

“To be completely honest, I felt a bit embarrassed, so I couldn’t really show my expressions or change my face much,” he explained.

Standing on the podium, he bowed slightly as he received his gold medal and gave a small wave to the arena.

“I’m really happy. The gold medal is really beautiful, shiny and heavy,” he said.

“Also, the plush toy is super cute, and it’s cool that it is gold-coloured too.”

Kurihara started playing Puyo Puyo in his first year of primary school and soon started competing and winning in tournaments. He obtained his pro licence in April this year and regularly beats adults.

“It’s hard having to balance it with school and cram school, but it’s really fun,” he said ahead of the games.

There are no publicly available records of the youngest medallists in the history of the Asian Games, which were first contested in 1951.

But Indonesia’s Bunga Nyimas won bronze in women’s skateboarding aged 12 in Jakarta in 2018.

Cui Chenxi, 13, won games gold when she triumphed in the women’s street skateboarding event three years ago in Hangzhou.

articles.title: Senegal draw in Vieira debut, Nigeria survive scare, but Cape Verde crash
articles.summary: Senegal draw with Mozambique, Nigeria edge past Madagascar, but Cape Verde beaten by Mali in AFCON qualifying openers.
articles.body:
Former France star Patrick Vieira debuted as Senegal coach by drawing 1-1 in Mozambique, and Nigeria survived a scare to edge Madagascar 2-1 in Africa Cup of Nations qualifying on Friday.

Cape Verde, admired for holding eventual 2026 World Cup winners Spain and taking Argentina to extra time before bowing out, crashed 3-1 away to Mali.

Egypt were held 0-0 at home by Angola while Morocco and Algeria won comfortably against Gabon and Zambia respectively.

Aston Villa striker Nicolas Jackson put controversial 2026 AFCON runners-up Senegal ahead after 32 minutes with a close-range tap off a low cross.

But Geny Catamo from Portuguese giants Sporting levelled in first-half added time, firing a shot from outside the box through a crowded goalmouth into the far corner of the net.

Senegal had plenty of second-half possession in Maputo, but could not find a way past a well-organised Mozambican defence.

Originally scheduled for Senegal, the matchday one fixture in Group J was moved to Maputo as no stadium in the West African nation currently meets international standards.

Vieira, 50, was a midfielder in the French teams that won the 1998 World Cup and 2000 European Championship, and also starred for Arsenal.

But he has had less success as a coach with clubs in the United States, France, England and Italy. He left Genoa last November with the club winless and bottom of Serie A.

Dakar-born Vieira has inherited from sacked Pape Thiaw a Senegal team in transition during a dramatic year in which they were stripped of the AFCON title and flopped at the World Cup.

The Teranga Lions temporarily walked off the pitch to protest a penalty awarded in the AFCON final to hosts Morocco, who missed the kick when Senegal returned.

Senegal won 1-0 after extra time only for the African confederation CAF to later award Morocco a 3-0 victory.

An appeal by the West Africans against the decision will be heard by the Court of Arbitration for Sport on October 8.

After losing to France and Norway at the World Cup, Senegal hammered Iraq to squeeze into the round of 32, where they fell to Belgium after surrendering a two-goal lead.

Against Mozambique, Senegal were without recently retired goalkeeper Edouard Mendy and injured striker Sadio Mane. Fellow stalwarts Kalilou Koulibaly and Idrissa Gueye were on the bench.

Nigeria, shock non-qualifiers for the past two World Cups, fell behind at home to Madagascar when Ehsan Kari scored after 16 minutes in Uyo.

A Super Eagles side lacking injured star striker Victor Osimhen were then rescued by two international debutants.

Saudi Arabia-based George Ilenikhena, 20, burst through to equalise in first-half added time and substitute Moses Usor from Austrian champions LASK snatched the 65th-minute winner.

Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha, a star at the World Cup, gifted Mali their third goal in the defeat before a wildly excited crowd of 50,000 in Bamako.

He dashed outside his area to control the ball with his chest, then lost possession and Dorgeles Nene struck the loose ball into an unguarded net.

Mali, arguably the strongest football nation never to win the AFCON, dominated from start to finish and led within five minutes through Martial Tia.

Cape Verde levelled when a Sidny Cabral free-kick was deflected into the net. Mali regained the lead as half-time approached through Nene.

articles.title: La DGT elimina dos excepciones históricas para los taxistas y los ciclistas: "Hay que dar ejemplo"
articles.standfirst: El cinturón de seguridad y el casco va a ser aún más obligatorio que antes para todos los colectivos
articles.summary: El cinturón de seguridad y el casco va a ser aún más obligatorio que antes para todos los colectivos
articles.body: El 1 de octubre entrarán en vigor varias normas nuevas del Reglamento General de Circulación. Una batería de cambios que van a afectar a todos los elementos que intervienen en el tráfico en nuestras carreteras. Hay dos de ellas que van a cambiar ciertos 'privilegios' que tenían algunos colectivos... que el mismísimo Pere Navarro, director general de Tráfico, ha justificado en una reciente comparecencia ante los medios. La próxima semana ya no veremos algo que estaba contemplado en la normativa de Tráfico española: a algunos conductores sin tener obligación de abrocharse el cinturón de seguridad. Se trata de los taxistas, a los que se eximía mientras circulaban por la ciudad, a los profesores de autoescuela y a los conductores de vehículos de reparto. Ahora ya no dispondrán de esa prebenda. Y el propio Pere Navarro ha explicado el motivo de estos cambios: "Los taxistas se quejan por eliminar la exención de uso del cinturón. Pero no vamos a conseguir que los pasajeros lleven el cinturón de seguridad si el conductor no lo lleva. Es un tema evidente", argumenta. La DGT considera que no es válido el argumento esgrimido por los taxistas, que apelan a su seguridad personal en una situación de atraco. Al menos no para sus competencias: "Que haya robos es un tema de seguridad ciudadana, pero no de seguridad vial. Nuestra responsabilidad es la responsabilidad vial, y el uso del cinturón es lógico, ¡Dios mío!", lanzó el máximo responsable de tráfico en España. En el caso de los profesores de autoescuela, la argumentación de Tráfico es similar: "También los profesores de autoescuela tienen que llevarlo, tienen que dar ejemplo", zanjó. Otro aspecto importante que cambiará desde ahora afectará a los ciclistas y al uso del casco. Hasta ahora, ese elemento era obligatorio... en casi todos los supuestos. Porque los artículos 118.1 y 119.3 del Reglamento establecen que habría dispensa a esta norma en los casos de que estén circulando por rampas ascendentes prolongadas y en condiciones extremas de calor (también por razones médicas debidamente acreditadas). Pero desde el 1 de octubre el calor y los puertos de montaña ya no serán excusa para no llevar casco. "Hasta los ciclistas profesionales lo llevan", explicaba un Pere Navarro que fue rotundo: "Incluso aunque haga mucho calor o haga mucha subida, hemos suprimido esta excepción. El casco será obligatorio".

articles.title: Luke Littler can become the greatest darts player ever – but may never surpass Phil Taylor, says Stephen Bunting
articles.summary: Stephen Bunting believes Luke Littler's ceiling means he has the potential to go down as the greatest darts player of all time; the two-time world championship semi-finalist spoke to Sky Sports News ahead of the launch of his new book 'Bulletproof'
articles.body:
Littler had been on course for a clean sweep of the 2026 ranking events before a shock exit at the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam .

The world No 1 had won the first six premier events of the season after following his World Championship triumph at Alexandra Palace in January with the World Masters, UK Open, Premier League, World Cup of Darts and World Matchplay.

Littler was hoping to add the World Series of Darts Finals, World Grand Prix, European Championship, Grand Slam of Darts and Players Championship Finals trophies to complete a historic monopoly over the year - but lost to Jonny Clayton in the quarter-finals .

Despite defeat, many experts are already predicting the 19-year-old becoming the greatest player the sport has ever seen - including Bunting.

"I do," the 41-year-old told Sky Sports News when asked if he thinks Littler can end his career as the greatest darts player ever. "I think he's got a lot more to give the sport."

However, Bunting believes darts legend Taylor, who retired in 2018, will still have the edge over Littler when it comes to the number of titles won.

"I think he'll win a lot more world titles, but I don't think he'll win as many as Phil," he said. "The standard of play is a lot better than in Phil's day. Phil did dominate.

"But [Littler] is someone who has changed our sport. He's brought the [age] demographic of the sport down. If you ask people who a darts player is, they all say Luke Littler, that's how powerful his name is."

Bunting did admit, however, that he would rather leave the debate over who is the best to Taylor and Littler themselves.

"I think certainly Luke's ceiling is phenomenal," he continued. "Based on his ceiling he is the best player in the world. Phil 'The Power' Taylor won 16 World Championships - you can't take that away from Phil.

"If Phil tells me he's the best darts player in the world, he's the best darts player in the world. I'll leave it for them to discuss. I'd be happy to win one or two world titles, but Luke is smashing it already.

"He's playing fantastic, won another European Tour, so he's pretty unstoppable. But there's a couple of players behind him who can also have high ceilings as well, so on the day, who knows what can happen."

Speaking on Love The Darts podcast, Bunting addressed Littler being booed and whistled at during the World Series of Darts Finals where he was asked whether it has gone too far.

"A loud whistle really does throw you off and I've had it in my career. It's not nice and it's off-putting when you're throwing for a double," said Bunting. "It's the minority."

Bunting will be competing at the World Grand Prix where he will be looking to go one step further after making the semi-finals twice previously.

"Definitely," Bunting said when asked if he can win the title in Leicester. "Hopefully I can go in with some really good form, these next few tournaments push me there with some confidence.

"The Grand Prix is a double-off format, I really enjoy hitting my doubles. It's going to be a great tournament. It's brilliant Sky Sports covers it and hopefully I can put on a good show for the fans and get the title."

As well as watching Bunting in full flow, fans at Leicester's Mattioli Arena will be excited when he walks out to his song 'Titanium'.

"My son's favourite song," Bunting said when asked about his song change. "It was an easy one to pick. I wanted to get away from the Peter Griffin and the 'Bird is the Word' song. Everyone's been really positive towards it.

"It's one of the greatest walk-on songs in my opinion. It's really a special moment when I'm doing the actions and they're singing it back to me. It makes me feel so happy.

"Obviously, we're up there to do a job and play darts, but the walk-on and the crowd takes the pressure away and it relaxes me when I've done the walk-on.

"When the crowd are singing 'let's go Bunting-mental', they really are my 12th man. To be able to use the crowd as a power, it's really important, they're a huge part of my game and it's nice to be able to give something back to them."

Bunting opens up on dark side of social media and gambling in 'Bulletproof'

Bunting spoke to Sky Sports News ahead of the launch of his new book 'Bulletproof', with the autobiography's title a nod to the lyrics in 'Titanium' and his nickname - but also about his battle to refuse to give up his darts.

"Sometimes it can be really difficult," Bunting admitted when asked about the hate he can receive on social media. "I'm lucky I've got a great team around me, a brilliant family and some unbelievable fans and they've really helped me through a little bit of a dark time.

"It came off the back of the 'people's champion' debacle, which was taken well out of context. I've put that all behind me now. It's about rebuilding again. The confidence is high, even though the results are not going my way at the minute, I'm sure that's about to change.

"It was important to show everyone, this was a life story, so, everything needs to be in there," he said. "The gambling debts were a big part of my life.

"When times were low, I'd lock myself away, and I'd be on my phone gambling. It was a horrible place to be in. I was in a rut and thankfully, sports psychologist, hypnotist and everything about that really helped me and helped me look at it in a positive way, even though somethings may not be positive, still taking a positive spin on it.

"Gambling was a way out at the time but I was able to put that to bed and if one little bit out of this book can help anyone in this situation, the book's a winner."

articles.title: Melilla se convierte en la capital del deporte con los Juegos del Agua
articles.standfirst: Este evento, organizado por ADESP, la Ciudad Autónoma y 11 Federaciones deportivas, acogerá varias disciplinas, como natación, vela, triatlón, surf, vela...
articles.summary: Este evento, organizado por ADESP, la Ciudad Autónoma y 11 Federaciones deportivas, acogerá varias disciplinas, como natación, vela, triatlón, surf, vela...
articles.body: Melilla se prepara para convertirse en el gran foco del Deporte acuático en nuestro país desde hoy hasta el 18 de octubre. Los II Juegos del Agua, organizados por la Asociación del Deporte Español (ADESP), la Ciudad Autónoma y 11 Federaciones Deportivas Españolas, reunirán durante 23 días a más de 3.000 deportistas, técnicos y jueces, que desplegarán un programa con nueve competiciones oficiales y dos exhibiciones en seis escenarios de la ciudad. El calendario incluye campeonatos de Europa, campeonatos y copas de España, y disciplinas tan diversas como la natación, el surfing, la vela, el triatlón, el piragüismo, la pesca, el salvamento, el pentatlón moderno, las actividades subacuáticas, el freestyle de motonáutica y el esquí náutico. La competición arranca este domingo con la etapa final de la XI Copa de España de Aguas Abiertas Open y continuará con una programación que convertirá las playas, el puerto deportivo, la Plaza de las Culturas y el Real Club Marítimo de Melilla en espacios de competición y encuentro. Entre las citas más destacadas figuran el Campeonato de Europa de Selecciones Nacionales de Stand Up Paddle, el Campeonato de Europa de Triatlón Youth, la Copa de España de Raceboard y los campeonatos de España de rescate en moto acuática, Triatle, caza foto apnea, barco dragón y pesca desde kayak. Los Juegos del Agua buscan posicionar Melilla como destino de turismo deportivo, generar impacto económico y social, impulsar la sostenibilidad medioambiental y fortalecer la colaboración entre Federaciones e instituciones. El Consejero de Educación, Juventud y Deporte de la Ciudad Autónoma de Melilla, Miguel Ángel Fernández Bonnemaison, destacó que “los Juegos del Agua representan una apuesta decidida por el deporte como motor de promoción, convivencia y desarrollo para Melilla”. Por su parte, el Presidente de ADESP, José Hidalgo explicó que “Melilla tiene ante sí una oportunidad extraordinaria para seguir demostrando todo lo que puede ofrecer al deporte español. Los Juegos del Agua reúnen competición, territorio y talento en un mismo proyecto, y permiten que muchas Federaciones compartan una gran celebración que proyecta la ciudad como un destino preparado para acoger eventos deportivos de alto nivel”. Como embajadores, los campeones mundiales Iballa Ruano y Mario Mola aportan dos miradas vinculadas al mar y al alto rendimiento. “Melilla ofrece un escenario magnífico para acercar los Deportes de agua a la ciudadanía y para que nuevas generaciones descubran todo lo que pueden encontrar en ellos”, asegura Ruano. Mola, cuatro veces campeón mundial, señala que “es muy especial que un proyecto reúna tantas disciplinas y Federaciones, porque demuestra la enorme riqueza del deporte acuático, los entornos naturales que ofrece Melilla y permite que la competición se viva también más allá de la ciudad”. Los Juegos del Agua podrán seguirse íntegramente a través del canal de Youtube de MARCA con toda la información en MARCA y MARCA.com. l

articles.body: NEW DELHI: India completed a golden double in kabaddi at the Asian Games 2026 on Saturday as the men’s team defeated Iran 40-34 in a thrilling final, hours after the women had also beaten the same opponents to retain their title.The men’s victory at Aichi-Nagoya earned India its ninth Asian Games gold in men’s kabaddi and successfully defended the title won at the Hangzhou edition. The two kabaddi gold medals also lifted India’s overall medal tally to 28 — four gold, 11 silver and 13 bronze, taking the country into the top 10 of the standings.It was another tense encounter against Iran, the 2018 Asian Games champions, with neither side able to establish sustained control for long periods. But India held their nerve through a roller-coaster second half before pulling away late to secure the gold.Asian Games Full Coverage | Medal Tally | ScheduleIndia and Iran trade blows in tense finalThe final began on an even note, with the teams locked at 5-5 after the opening eight minutes. India then managed to create a small advantage, moving 12-9 ahead, but Iran responded strongly and turned the contest around.With less than five minutes remaining in the first half, Iran moved ahead 14-13. India responded by reclaiming the advantage at 16-14, only for Iran to strike back again.The momentum continued to swing between the two sides, and Iran eventually went into the interval with an 18-17 lead.India needed a strong response after the restart, but Iran extended their advantage to 20-17. A crucial super tackle helped India cut the deficit to 19-20 before the defending champions finally regained the lead at 21-20.Iran immediately levelled at 21-21, underlining just how little separated the two teams.India then began to build some breathing room, moving 24-21 ahead. Iran responded with a super tackle of their own to collect two points and reduce India's advantage to 24-23.The match remained finely balanced, but India produced the crucial breakthrough with an all-out that pushed them five points clear at 29-24 with 10 minutes remaining.Men follow women to complete golden doubleFrom there, India managed the contest effectively. Iran continued to push for a comeback, but the Indian defence held firm and the attack kept adding points to maintain the advantage.India eventually closed out the final 40-34 to complete the kabaddi double and retain the men's title.The result also gave India its fourth gold of the Games and moved the country into the top 10 of the overall medal standings.Earlier on Saturday, the Indian women's kabaddi team had set the stage for the double by overcoming Iran 37-34 in another closely fought final.The women, too, successfully defended the gold they had won at Hangzhou. India held their nerve during a tense closing phase as Iran attempted to force a late comeback.With only a minute remaining, Iran needed points to remain in contention, but India's defence produced a crucial tackle on Aynaz to effectively seal the contest.India eventually prevailed 37-34, with Sanju Devi once again playing a key role after being one of the team's standout performers throughout the tournament.For Indian kabaddi, it was a statement day: two finals against Iran, two victories and two gold medals, with both the men's and women's teams successfully defending their Asian Games titles.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Virat Kohli says he will retire from India cricket after 2027 World Cup
articles.summary: The leading century-maker in ODI cricket, Virat Kohli, announces 2027 World Cup will be his swansong for India.
articles.body:
Virat Kohli said next ‌year’s 50-over World Cup would be his last for India and he ⁠is ready to ⁠give his all to help lift the trophy.

The leading century-maker in ODIs with 54 hundreds, has already retired from T20 internationals and Test cricket ⁠and now only represents India in the 50-over format.

The 37-year-old batter, who has scored 14,941 runs in one-day internationals, second only to Sachin Tendulkar’s 18,426, won ⁠the World Cup on home soil in 2011 before suffering defeat in the 2023 final against Australia.

The 2027 edition, to be jointly hosted by South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia in October to November, will be Kohli’s fifth ODI World Cup.

“For me, it’s the ‌last World Cup I’m going to play for India,” Kohli told broadcaster JioStar on Saturday.

“That is my motivation and like, you know, to leave everything out there. And of course, the goal is absolutely to win the World Cup and whatever it takes, I’m absolutely ready.”

Kohli said the demands of a 50-over World Cup made it one of cricket’s toughest challenges, particularly with the ⁠tournament set to be played away from home.

“The intensity of ⁠a 50-over World Cup is greater than anything. Because now, it’s about 10 games at a Twenty20 level of intensity,” he said.

“But you are playing 2.5 T20 games in one day. And to maintain ⁠that intensity for 10 games in a big tournament and World Cup is a big deal. Also now, it’s in ⁠foreign conditions. It takes a lot out of ⁠you.”

Former captain Rohit Sharma, who also plays only ODIs for India, said he remained fully motivated by the prospect of another World Cup campaign.

“The thought will never cross my mind that the business I ‌had is finished,” Rohit said.

“As long as you’re playing, there is always something to look forward to. And I’m looking forward to the World Cup.”

Kohli and Rohit were ‌both ‌named in India’s squad for the three-match ODI series against West Indies. The opening match will be played in Thiruvananthapuram on Sunday.

articles.title: Mr. Olympia 2026 Full Event Schedule and Historic Info on Past Winners
articles.summary: The top trophy in men's bodybuilding will be awarded on Saturday night when Joe Weider's Fitness and Performance Weekend culminates with the finals of the Mr. Olympia Open competition.
articles.body:
The top trophy in men's bodybuilding will be awarded on Saturday night when Joe Weider's Fitness and Performance Weekend culminates with the finals of the Mr. Olympia Open competition.

The Open—typically referred to as the Mr. Olympia—has been the marquee event in men's bodybuilding since its inception in 1965. Over the years, it has been won by some of the biggest legends in the sport, and it has often been dominated for long stretches by these larger-than-life figures.

This year, reigning champion Derek Lunsford will look to earn another piece of history and join some of these legends by lifting his third Sandow Trophy in four years. To do it, though, he'll have to fend off the best pros the International Fitness and Bodybuilding Federation (IFBB) has to offer.

Here's a quick look at the history of the Mr. Olympia, a rundown of the remaining schedule, and a preview of Saturday's finals.

International Sports Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony

Arnold Schwarzenegger is arguably still the face of professional bodybuilding, at least to the casual fan, thanks to his successful transition to Hollywood entertainment. His Arnold Sports Festival, held annually in Columbus, has also become a marquee event, headlined by the Arnold Classic, which nearly rivals the Mr. Olympia in its profile.

However, the Olympia is still the gold standard of IFBB competition and has been since Weider founded it. Schwarzenegger was the third champion crowned, following Larry Scott (1965-66) and Sergio Olivia (1967-69). Schwarzenegger won the Olympia six straight years before making a comeback win in 1980.

While Schwarzenegger does hold the record for the youngest Mr. Olympia ever (23 years, 2 months), he does not hold the record for the most victories. That record stands at eight and is shared by Lee Haney and Ronnie Coleman.

Shawn Rhoden holds the record for the oldest Mr. Olympia at 43 years and five months.

Haney, Coleman, Olivia, Schwarzenegger, Frank Zane, Dorian Yates, Jay Cutler, and Phil Heath make up the list of competitors who have won the Mr. Olympia three or more times. That's the group that Lunsford is looking to join this weekend.

Lunsford is also looking to become the first repeat champion since Mamdouh Elssibay won in 2020 and 2021.

The reigning champ will have to fend off 2024 Olympia winner Samson Dauda and 2026 Arnold Classic winner Andrew Jacked to retain the title. Other top competitors like Nick Walker and Martin Fitzwater should have a chance to make an impression at the finals as well.

In all, 22 IFBB pros qualified for the 2026 Olympia Open.

The finals are scheduled to begin around 7 p.m. local time (10 p.m. ET) at the Orleans Arena in Las Vegas. Fans hoping to catch the action from home can follow the live stream at OlympiaProductions.com .
